concepts.name: Electric current
concepts.statement: Electric current is the rate at which charge flows. A large current, such as the one that starts a truck engine, moves a large amount of charge in a small time, while a small current, such as the one that runs a handheld calculator, moves a small amount of charge over a long time. Because current is a rate rather than an amount, the same idea describes a lightning bolt and a clock battery, and every other result in the chapter builds on it.

concepts.name: Ampere
concepts.statement: Since current is a charge divided by a time, its SI unit is one coulomb per second, named the ampere for the French physicist André-Marie Ampère. Fuses, circuit breakers and many electrical appliances carry ratings in amperes.

concepts.name: Conventional current
concepts.statement: The direction of conventional current is the direction that positive charge would flow. Depending on the situation, positive charges, negative charges, or both may move. In metal wires electrons carry the current, in ionic solutions such as salt water both signs move, and a Van de Graaff generator can produce a current of pure positive charges. One convention lets the same circuit analysis apply whatever the carriers are. Keep in mind that the electrons in a wire actually move opposite to the current drawn on the diagram.

concepts.name: Reading a circuit schematic
concepts.statement: A schematic represents a battery by two parallel lines, a conducting wire by a straight line and a load by a zigzag, and a single schematic can stand for anything from a truck battery lighting a headlight to a small battery lighting a keyhole. Schematics are useful because the analysis is the same for a wide variety of situations, so understanding a few of them lets the reader apply the concepts to many more.

concepts.name: Charge carriers
concepts.statement: Current is the flow of free charges, and which charges are free depends on the material. In a metal the free charges are electrons far enough from their nuclei to move among the atoms in a sea, while in an ionic solution or a nerve cell ions of both signs move. A conductor carrying a current has an electric field in it, which supplies the energy to move the charges. It is therefore not in static equilibrium, as the conductors of the previous two chapters were.

concepts.name: Drift velocity
concepts.statement: The drift velocity is the average velocity of the free charges in a conductor. An individual electron moves quickly and almost at random, colliding with atoms and with other electrons, but an electric field tilts that random walk so that the whole crowd creeps one way. The drift velocity is quite small, on the order of $10^{-4}$ m/s, because there are so many free charges: the larger the density of carriers, the lower the velocity needed to carry a given current.

concepts.name: Signal speed versus drift
concepts.statement: Electrical signals travel at speeds on the order of $10^{8}$ m/s, about $10^{12}$ times the drift velocity of the charges that carry them. The force between charges acts rapidly at a distance, and that reconciles the two speeds. A charge forced into one end of a wire pushes the charges ahead of it, which push on charges farther down the line. The signal is a rapidly propagating change in electric field, not the arrival of any particular electron.

concepts.name: Current and drift velocity
concepts.statement: Counting the free charges in a segment of wire gives the current directly. A segment of cross-sectional area $A$ and length $x$ holds $nAx$ carriers of charge $q$ each, and if they all leave the segment in a time $\Delta t$, the current is that charge divided by that time. Since $x/\Delta t$ is the drift velocity, the current is $I = nqAv_\text{d}$. This ties the number you measure with an ammeter to the microscopic picture of a crowd of electrons.

concepts.name: Ohm’s law
concepts.statement: Georg Simon Ohm was the first to demonstrate experimentally that the current in a metal wire is directly proportional to the voltage applied to it. Combining that proportionality with the fact that current is inversely proportional to resistance gives $I = V/R$, which can be read as a cause-and-effect relationship with voltage the cause and current the effect. It is the relation the rest of the chapter, and the whole of circuit analysis, rests on.

concepts.name: Resistance
concepts.statement: If voltage drives current, something must impede it, and that electric property is called resistance. Collisions of moving charges with the atoms and molecules of a substance transfer energy to the substance and limit the current, so current is inversely proportional to resistance and is cut in half if the resistance doubles. Resistances range over many orders of magnitude, from $10^{-5}\;\Omega$ for a meter of thick copper wire to $10^{12}\;\Omega$ for a ceramic insulator.

concepts.name: Ohm
concepts.statement: The unit of resistance is one volt per ampere, which is named the ohm and written with the capital Greek omega, $1\;\Omega = 1\;\text{V/A}$. An object that has simple resistance is called a resistor, even when its resistance is small.

concepts.name: Ohmic materials
concepts.statement: Ohm's law, like Hooke's law, is not universally valid. The many substances for which it holds are called ohmic, and they include good conductors like copper and aluminum and some poor conductors under certain circumstances; an ohmic material has a resistance that does not depend on the voltage across it or the current through it. Knowing that the law is empirical rather than fundamental tells the reader when a straight line through the origin is the right model and when it is not.

concepts.name: Simple circuit
concepts.statement: A simple circuit has a single voltage source and a single resistor, with the connecting wires assumed to have negligible resistance or their resistance included in $R$. It is the smallest complete circuit there is, and settling how voltage, current and resistance behave in it is what makes the more complicated circuits of the next chapter tractable.

concepts.name: IR drop
concepts.statement: Solving Ohm's law for the voltage gives $V = IR$, the voltage drop across a resistor produced by the current flowing through it, often called the $IR$ drop. Measure the voltage at various points in a circuit and you find that it increases at the voltage source and decreases at the resistor. In a simple circuit the same charge flows through each, so conservation of energy requires the voltage supplied by the source to equal the voltage dropped across the resistor.

concepts.name: Resistivity
concepts.statement: For a given shape, the resistance depends on the material the object is made of, and the resistivity is the property that carries that dependence. Resistivity is an intrinsic property of a material, independent of its shape or size, and its unit is the ohm-meter.

concepts.name: Resistance of a cylinder
concepts.statement: The resistance of a uniform cylinder is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, just as the resistance a pipe offers to fluid flow is: the longer the cylinder, the more collisions the charges make with its atoms, and the greater its diameter, the more current it can carry. With the resistivity of the material this gives the resistance of any simple shape from its dimensions alone.

concepts.name: Conductors, semiconductors and insulators
concepts.statement: The materials of Table 20.1 fall into three groups by their resistivities. Conductors have the smallest resistivities and varying but large free charge densities; insulators have the largest, because most of their charges are bound to atoms and are not free to move; and semiconductors are intermediate, having far fewer free charges than conductors but a number of free charges that depends strongly on the type and amount of impurities present. That last property is what modern electronics is built on.

concepts.name: Superconductivity
concepts.statement: The resistivity of all materials depends on temperature, and some become superconductors, with zero resistivity, at very low temperatures. A sample of mercury has no resistance at all up to about 4.2 K, and above that critical temperature its resistance makes a sudden jump and then increases nearly linearly. A material with no resistance carries a steady current with no continual supply of energy, which is why the possibility matters far beyond the laboratory.

concepts.name: Temperature coefficient of resistivity
concepts.statement: The temperature coefficient of resistivity is the empirical quantity that describes how much a material's resistivity changes with temperature. It is positive for metals, because at higher temperatures their atoms vibrate more rapidly and over larger distances, so the electrons make more collisions. It is negative for the semiconductors of Table 20.2, because increased thermal agitation there frees more charges to carry current. Some alloys, such as manganin, have a coefficient close to zero, which makes them ideal for a temperature-independent resistance standard.

concepts.name: Resistivity and temperature
concepts.statement: Over relatively small temperature changes, about 100 °C or less, the resistivity varies linearly with the temperature change, where $\rho_0$ is the original resistivity and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient. For larger changes the coefficient may itself vary or a nonlinear equation may be needed, so treat the linear form as the approximation it is.

concepts.name: Resistance and temperature
concepts.statement: Since the resistance of a cylinder is proportional to the resistivity, and since the length and the area change far less with temperature than the resistivity does, the resistance of an object has the same temperature dependence as the resistivity. Numerous thermometers are based on this effect, the most common being the thermistor, a semiconductor crystal with a strong temperature dependence whose resistance is measured to obtain its temperature.

concepts.name: Electric power
concepts.statement: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is supplied by a source or dissipated by a device. Since electric energy is $\text{PE} = qV$, the power is the charge per second times the voltage, which is the current times the voltage, $P = IV$. One ampere-volt is one watt.

concepts.name: Power and resistance
concepts.statement: Substituting Ohm's law into $P = IV$ gives two further expressions, and each yields its own insight. The first says that the lower the resistance connected to a given voltage source, the greater the power delivered. Because the voltage is squared, raising it has a larger effect than expected, which is why a 25-W bulb connected to 240 V glows brightly and burns out. The second is the form to use when the current rather than the voltage is fixed, as in a transmission line. The first expression is always valid; these two can be used only for resistors.

concepts.name: Power supplied and dissipated
concepts.statement: In a circuit with one voltage source and a single resistor, the power supplied by the source and the power dissipated by the resistor are identical, because the resistor is the only place the energy can go. In more complicated circuits $P$ may be the power dissipated by a single device rather than the total power in the circuit, so always say which power you mean.

concepts.name: Electrical energy and cost
concepts.statement: Since power is energy per unit time, the energy a device uses is its power multiplied by the time it is on, and that is what appears on an electric bill. The energy unit on electric bills is the kilowatt-hour, which is $3.6\times10^{6}$ J, and the cost of running anything can be estimated from its power rating in kilowatts, the hours it is on and the cost per kilowatt-hour.

concepts.name: Lighting efficiency
concepts.statement: You can reduce the electrical energy used either by shortening the time of use or by lowering the power consumption. Lighting is one of the fastest places to do it, since it takes about 20 per cent of a home's energy use and closer to 40 per cent of a commercial building's. Fluorescent lights are about four times more efficient than incandescent lights and last up to ten times longer. White LED lights are about twice as efficient again and last five times longer than compact fluorescents.

concepts.name: Direct current
concepts.statement: Direct current is the flow of electric charge in only one direction, and it is the steady state of a constant-voltage circuit such as one driven by a battery. Naming it is what makes the contrast with alternating current sharp, and most of the examples of the chapter so far have been of this kind.

concepts.name: Alternating current
concepts.statement: Alternating current is the flow of electric charge that periodically reverses direction, and when the source varies sinusoidally the circuit is an alternating current circuit. The voltage between the terminals is $V = V_0\sin 2\pi ft$, where $V_0$ is the peak voltage and $f$ the frequency in hertz. In a simple resistance circuit the current follows it in phase as $I = I_0\sin 2\pi ft$ with $I_0 = V_0/R$. Most of the commercial and residential power we use is of this kind.

concepts.name: Average AC power
concepts.statement: Since the power supplied is the product of the current and the voltage and the two are in phase, the power is $I_0V_0\sin^2 2\pi ft$, which is never negative and fluctuates between zero and $I_0V_0$ twice in each cycle. We are most often concerned with the average rather than the fluctuation, and the average is half the peak, as is evident from the graph, since the areas above and below the half-peak line are equal.

concepts.name: rms current and voltage
concepts.statement: The ordinary average of an alternating current is zero, so we need a different kind of average: square the quantity, find its mean, and take the square root. The result is the root mean square. It is standard practice to quote the rms current and voltage and the average power rather than the peak values, so household electricity described as 120 V AC has an rms voltage of 120 V and a peak of about 170 V. Think of these as the equivalent DC values for a simple resistive circuit.

concepts.name: Ohm’s law for AC
concepts.statement: For alternating current, Ohm's law and the expressions for power are completely analogous to those for direct current, provided you use rms and average values throughout. That is what makes the rms average worth defining: with it, everything from 20.2 and 20.4 carries over unchanged.

concepts.name: High-voltage transmission
concepts.statement: Economies of scale make a few very large generating plants cheaper than many small ones, so power must travel long distances, and the energy lost on the way must be kept small. For a given power, raising the voltage lowers the current, and since the loss in a fixed-resistance line is $I^2R$, the loss falls as the square. 100 MW sent at 200 kV over a 1.00-Ω line loses a quarter of a per cent, while the same power at 25 kV loses 16 per cent. Alternating voltages are much easier to raise and lower than direct ones, which is why AC has prevailed in large-scale distribution.

concepts.name: AC voltage
concepts.statement: An AC voltage is a voltage that fluctuates sinusoidally with time, $V = V_0\sin 2\pi ft$, where $V_0$ is its peak value and $f$ its frequency.

concepts.name: rms current
concepts.statement: The rms current is the root mean square of an alternating current, $I_\text{rms} = I_0/\sqrt{2}$, where $I_0$ is the peak current.

concepts.name: rms voltage
concepts.statement: The rms voltage is the root mean square of an AC voltage, $V_\text{rms} = V_0/\sqrt{2}$, where $V_0$ is the peak voltage.

concepts.name: Thermal hazards
concepts.statement: A thermal hazard is one in which excessive electric power causes undesired thermal effects, such as starting a fire in the wall of a house. Electric power causes such heating whenever electric energy is converted to thermal energy faster than it can safely be dissipated, and naming the hazard separately from shock is what lets the reader see that the two are governed by different quantities.

concepts.name: Short circuit
concepts.statement: A short circuit is a low-resistance path between the terminals of a voltage source, such as the one made when worn insulation lets two wires touch. Because the resistance of the short is very small and the power dissipated in it is $V^2/r$, that power is very large: 120 V across 0.100 Ω gives 144 kW, far more than any household appliance uses, and thermal energy delivered at that rate very quickly melts or ignites the surrounding materials. Worse, the heating can ionize the material and lower the resistance further, raising the power again.

concepts.name: Overloaded wires
concepts.statement: A less dramatic thermal hazard occurs when the wires supplying a user carry too great a current, since the power dissipated in them is $I^2R_\text{w}$: a worn cord with 2.00 Ω rather than the 0.100 Ω it should have dissipates 200 W when 10.0 A passes through it. Fuses and circuit breakers limit such currents by opening the circuit automatically when a sustained current exceeds safe limits, a fuse by melting a metal strip and a breaker by bending a bimetallic strip that trips a spring.

concepts.name: Shock hazards
concepts.statement: A shock hazard occurs when electric current passes through a person, and the effects range from painful but otherwise harmless to heart-stopping. Current through people is not always harmful and is sometimes useful, since it can block back pain, burn off warts, drive a pacemaker or bring a heart out of fibrillation; what decides the outcome is the amount of the current, the path it takes, the duration of the shock and the frequency of the current.

concepts.name: Effects of current on the body
concepts.statement: Once the path, duration and frequency are fixed, current is the major factor determining the severity of a shock. The threshold of sensation is only 1 mA, and shocks below 5 mA are apparently harmless. From 10 to 20 mA the current stimulates sustained muscular contraction, so the hand closes on the wire and cannot let go. Between 100 and 300 mA ventricular fibrillation is possible and often fatal, and above about 300 mA burns begin. At several amperes the heart and diaphragm contract for the duration of the shock and often return to normal afterwards, which is how a defibrillator works. The body is most sensitive near the 50 and 60 Hz in common use and becomes progressively less sensitive at higher frequencies.

concepts.name: Body resistance and microshock
concepts.statement: A larger voltage is more hazardous, but since $I = V/R$ the severity of a shock depends on the combination of voltage and resistance, so no voltage is hazardous without knowing the resistance. Most of the body's resistance is in its dry skin, about 200 kΩ hand to foot, and 120 V drives only 0.6 mA through it. The same person soaking wet may have 10.0 kΩ and take 12 mA, above the can't-let-go threshold. When an intravenous infusion, a catheter or exposed pacemaker leads bypass the skin, the person is microshock sensitive, and currents about a thousandth of those in Table 20.3 produce similar effects.

concepts.name: Microshock sensitivity
concepts.statement: A person is microshock sensitive when the resistance of the skin is bypassed, possibly by a medical procedure, so that a very small current can reach the heart.

concepts.name: Resting potential
concepts.statement: A cell membrane separates electrically neutral fluids whose concentrations of sodium, potassium and chlorine ions differ, and it is semipermeable, passing potassium and chlorine in the resting state but not sodium. Diffusion carries those ions across until the layers of charge they build up stop further transfer by the Coulomb force, leaving two layers of charge right on the membrane and a potential difference of 70 to 90 mV across it. Because the membrane is only about 8 nm thick, that small voltage makes a field on the order of 11 MV/m, which has fundamental effects on the membrane's structure and permeability.

concepts.name: Action potential
concepts.statement: Any stimulus that changes the membrane's permeability creates a current along it. The membrane becomes temporarily permeable to sodium, which rushes in driven both by diffusion and by the Coulomb force and first neutralizes and then reverses the inside of the membrane, which is depolarization; the depolarization closes the membrane to sodium again and the movement of potassium returns the cell to its resting potential, which is repolarization. The sequence is a voltage pulse called the action potential, and only small fractions of the ions move, so the cell can fire hundreds of times before the sodium-potassium pump must restore the concentrations by active transport.

concepts.name: How a nerve impulse propagates
concepts.statement: An action potential is a voltage pulse at one place on a membrane, and the changing voltage and electric fields there alter the permeability of the adjacent membrane, so the same process happens next door, and then farther down. The result is a nerve impulse that moves along the cell membrane at about 1 m/s, slowly in electrical terms, and although it is due to sodium and potassium crossing the membrane it is equivalent to a wave of charge moving along the outside and inside of it.

concepts.name: Myelin sheath
concepts.statement: Myelin, a fatty insulator broken by unmyelinated gaps called nodes of Ranvier, sheathes some axons. Because myelin is an insulator, it keeps signals from jumping between adjacent nerves. The myelinated regions carry the signal at high speed as an ordinary conductor would, with no action potential and so no cell energy used. There is an $IR$ signal loss in the myelin, but each gap restores the signal to full voltage. A myelinated axon therefore transmits an impulse faster, with less energy and with better protection from cross talk. Destruction of the sheaths impairs transmission, as it does in multiple sclerosis.

concepts.name: Electrocardiogram
concepts.statement: The depolarization that makes a muscle cell contract can stimulate the cells next to it, so a depolarization wave crosses the heart from the sinoatrial node and coordinates its rhythmic contractions. An electrocardiogram is a record of the voltages that wave and the repolarization after it create, read as vector components between pairs of electrodes on the body. In the lead II potential the P wave is the depolarization of the atria, the QRS complex the depolarization of the ventricles, and the T wave their repolarization, with the systolic blood pressure following shortly after the QRS complex.

concepts.name: Bioelectricity
concepts.statement: Bioelectricity is the electrical effects in and created by biological systems. Nerve cells carry electrical signals, and the currents that make muscles contract produce voltages that can be measured outside the body.
